cards.title: The no low-energy sampleable states conjecture
cards.formal: In the perfect-sampling-access model of Definition 5.1 and Conjecture 4 of Gharibian and Le Gall, do there exist a constant k, a family of k-local n-qubit Hamiltonians H_n with ||H_n||≤1, and ε>0 such that for every succinctly represented vector family F there is n₀(F) for which every n≥n₀(F) and every unit vector u∈F_n satisfy u†H_nu>λ_min(H_n)+ε? Here F_n consists of the vectors in F of dimension 2^n. The exact access requirements are expanded below; the numerical machine conventions still requiring specification are recorded explicitly.
cards.why: Tests whether low-energy spaces can exclude every succinct classical description that supports both amplitude queries and exact measurement sampling, complementing lower bounds based on quantum circuit depth.

cards.definitions: An n-qubit pure state is a unit vector u∈ℂ^(2^n), indexed by binary strings x∈{0,1}^n. A Hamiltonian is a Hermitian matrix; its energy in u is u†Hu, its ground energy λ_min(H) is its least eigenvalue, and ||H|| is its operator norm. A k-local Hamiltonian is a sum of polynomially many terms, each acting nontrivially on at most k qubits and as the identity on the rest. The constant k and the polynomial bound are independent of n. No geometric locality or efficient uniform construction of the Hamiltonian family is added to the source’s existence target. The norm bound fixes the energy scale, so multiplying all terms cannot create the required constant gap artificially. For a family F of nonzero finite complex vectors, a succinct representation consists of an injective map rep:F→{0,1}*, one polynomial q and one polynomial-time compiler A. Every u∈F has |rep(u)|≤q(log₂ dim u). On a valid representation A outputs descriptions of a coordinate-query procedure Q_u, a randomized sampler S_u, and m=||u||; on every string outside the image of rep it must reject. For any coordinate x, Q_u returns the complex amplitude u_x, including its phase, in time polynomial in log dim u. S_u produces x with probability exactly |u_x|²/||u||² in polynomial time. The resulting circuit descriptions have polynomial size in log dim u. This is the source’s perfect, ζ=0 access, with no approximation to the distribution or norm. The representation map itself need not be computable from an explicitly listed vector. The same polynomial bounds and compiler apply throughout F; the eventual threshold n₀ may depend on this entire representation family. The assertion tests every unit vector in F_n, not one preselected sequence of easy states. The source counts exact complex additions, subtractions, multiplications and divisions at unit cost; this is not automatically a bit-cost sampling model.
cards.answer_criterion: Resolve the stated source-model existence proposition with its ∃Hamiltonian family, ∃ε, ∀representation family, ∃n₀ quantifiers and perfect-sampling plus amplitude-query requirements. Before treating the card as a standalone machine-level benchmark, resolve the numerical conventions recorded in statement_review. Excluding only stabilizer states, Gaussian states or constant-depth quantum preparation does not exclude every family allowed by Definition 5.1.

context_blocks.title: Sampling outcomes loses phase information
context_blocks.text: The states |+⟩=(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 and |−⟩=(|0⟩−|1⟩)/√2 both produce a uniformly random bit when measured in the computational basis. Yet for H=(I−X)/2, where X exchanges |0⟩ and |1⟩, their energies are 0 and 1. Their measurement distributions agree while their energies differ. This is why the source also requires access to each complex amplitude.

context_blocks.title: What a succinct description must do
context_blocks.text: Listing all 2^n amplitudes would be exponentially long. A permitted description instead has length polynomial in n and supports the prescribed efficient queries and samples. The source further requires a common compiler that rejects invalid descriptions; it is not enough to assert that some sampler exists for each isolated state.

context_blocks.title: Why the threshold comes after the description family
context_blocks.text: Any particular finite state with suitable numerical data can be given a long description. The conjecture concerns asymptotic families with one polynomial bound, and allows the exclusion threshold to depend on that family. Requiring one fixed threshold to exclude every possible description polynomial at once would change the quantifiers.

context_blocks.title: NLTS and stabilizer exclusions address different properties
context_blocks.text: The proved NLTS theorem excludes preparation by constant-depth quantum circuits. NLSS instead excludes the specified classical query-and-sampling descriptions. Coble and coauthors exclude stabilizer states and can retain NLTS in the same construction, but stabilizer states form only one class with efficient classical descriptions. Their result does not establish the full NLSS target.

cards.title: Do p-optimal propositional proof systems exist?
cards.formal: Does there exist a Cook–Reckhow proof system P for propositional tautologies such that, for every Cook–Reckhow proof system Q for the same tautologies, there is a deterministic polynomial-time translation t_Q satisfying P(t_Q(π))=Q(π) for every finite binary proof string π?
cards.why: Asks whether one efficiently checkable proof formalism can efficiently absorb every other such formalism.

progress.text: Theorem 2.1(ii) relates polynomial simulation of all propositional proof systems to optimal tautology recognition and finite-consistency proof construction; P=NP implies this existence.
Q1 explicitly retains (p-)optimality for TAUT as open. New oracle constructions show barriers for relativizing answers even with assumptions about the polynomial hierarchy.
ICALP work on recursive jump operators gives oracle barriers and results for other languages, while retaining the propositional optimality questions.

cards.definitions: Fix an explicit binary syntax for Boolean formulas built from indexed variables, AND, OR and NOT. A tautology evaluates to true under every assignment to its variables; TAUT is the set of encodings of such formulas. A Cook–Reckhow proof system is a total function P:{0,1}*→TAUT, computed by one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in its input length, whose range is all of TAUT. A string π proves formula F when P(π)=F. Soundness requires every output to be a tautology; completeness requires every tautology to occur as an output. There is no polynomial upper bound on the shortest proof of every formula. In this total-function presentation, strings that would be malformed proofs in a conventional calculus may instead produce a fixed tautology such as x₁∨¬x₁. A simulation translation is total and satisfies the equality on all strings, preserving the exact output formula. Its program, polynomial exponent and constants may depend on Q and P, but not on π. The order is ∃P ∀Q ∃t_Q ∀π. No algorithm taking an arbitrary program for Q and producing its translator is required. Neither advice, randomization nor an oracle is allowed in the systems or translations. Polynomial translation time also bounds the translated proof length polynomially in |π|.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that one sound and complete polynomial-time proof system admits the required polynomial-time translations from every other such system, or prove that for every candidate P some sound and complete Q has no such translation. A proof-length comparison without an efficient translation proves only ordinary optimality. Refuting a particular named proof system’s p-optimality does not exclude all systems.

context_blocks.title: One common format for efficiently checked proofs
context_blocks.text: Different proof calculi can establish the same tautology with very different amounts of work. The question asks whether one format can accept a polynomial-time translation of any already-given proof in any other efficiently checkable format. The translator receives the proof; it is not being asked to discover a proof from the formula alone.

context_blocks.title: A simple simulation
context_blocks.text: Suppose Q is a proof system and another system merely adds a leading marker to each Q-proof. Removing the marker translates those proofs back with linear overhead. More generally, any fixed finite collection of sound systems can be combined using a system tag. The question quantifies over every sound polynomial-time system, so combining a predetermined finite list does not finish it.

context_blocks.title: Three distinct notions
context_blocks.text: Ordinary optimality asks only that comparably short proofs exist in the common system. P-optimality additionally asks for efficient translations of the given proofs. Polynomial boundedness instead asks that every tautology have a proof polynomial in the formula’s own length. A p-optimal system could still have very long proofs of some tautologies, so this target does not by itself say NP=coNP.

context_blocks.title: Known connections and current limits
context_blocks.text: Krajíček and Pudlák connect p-optimality with a tautology recognizer that is optimal up to polynomial overhead on positive inputs, compared with each other correct recognizer. Their theorem also gives the conditional implication from P=NP. Egidy’s February 2026 paper retains the question as open and proves limitations of relativizing arguments; the oracle supplied to those machines is extra computational power, absent from this card.

context_blocks.title: Later work on improving proof systems
context_blocks.text: The ICALP 2026 paper studies when the absence of an ordinary optimal system entails an effective procedure producing stronger systems. Its oracle and other-language results leave p-optimal propositional proof systems unresolved. Ordinary optimality, a procedure for improving systems, and efficient proof translation are related but separately quantified properties.

sentences: Does one propositional proof system efficiently translate proofs from every other efficiently checkable system?
The translation must preserve the proved formula and run in time polynomial in the given proof length.
Each simulated system may have its own translator and polynomial.
This is stronger than comparing proof lengths alone, and different from requiring short proofs of every tautology.
The 2026 oracle and jump-operator results leave the ordinary, oracle-free existence question open.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
